article:
(Sept 29): Delhi is imposing construction curbs, work-from-home rules and vehicle restrictions to combat the Indian capital’s annual winter air pollution crisis.

The measures, which take effect Nov 1, include a ban on dust-generating construction, a requirement for 50% of employees to work from home and restrictions on older, more polluting vehicles registered outside Delhi. The city will also double parking fees and step up enforcement against vehicles without valid pollution certificates. The measures will run through January.

India’s Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav and Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta met on Monday to review preparations and finalise measures under the city’s permanent Winter Pollution Master Plan, according to a government statement.

Every winter, falling temperatures trap vehicle exhaust, industrial emissions and smoke from crop burning over the national capital region, pushing Delhi into the ranks of the world’s most polluted major cities. The World Bank warns that severe air pollution can deter foreign investment and skilled talent.

The move highlights the mounting toll of toxic air on South Asia’s largest economy. Air pollution contributes to about two million deaths annually while Delhi residents could lose eight years of life expectancy from sustained exposure, according to University of Chicago research. Studies have estimated the economic cost at as much as 6% of GDP.

The fixed calendar aims to give residents and businesses more certainty than the existing Graded Response Action Plan, which imposes curbs as pollution worsens. The reactive approach has routinely led to sudden construction halts, traffic restrictions and operational disruptions for businesses with little advance warning.

See also: Tata Trusts propose restructuring of Tata Sons to avoid listing

The meeting also called for coordinated action with neighbouring states to curb crop-residue burning, a major contributor to Delhi’s winter smog. Authorities across the National Capital Region have been asked to finalise their plans by Oct 10.

Experts say the measures may not be enough to tackle some of the main causes of Delhi’s winter pollution. The plan largely consolidates existing restrictions and focuses on larger particulate matter, known as PM10, rather than PM2.5, the tiny particles from sources such as vehicle exhaust and burning fuels that pose a greater health risk, said Manoj Kumar, analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.

“While pre-setting dates gives the government buffer time, implementation is what matters — and this plan still has a lot of gaps,” Kumar said.

See also: India state firms pull US$688 mil of bond sales as yields rise

Ahead of the rollout, the government has directed officials to review 37 pollution hotspots, finish road repairs and deploy AI-enabled monitoring by mid-October.

title: Crypto hack spurs US$463 mil in customer outflows at Bitget
article:
(Sept 29): Hacked crypto exchange Bitget recorded roughly US$463 million in net outflows in the 24 hours into Tuesday as customers moved assets off the platform following last week’s US$388 million theft.

The surge came after Bitget began restoring withdrawals and marked the largest one-day net outflow since data aggregator DefiLlama began tracking proof-of-reserves four years ago. The exchange currently holds about US$5.7 billion in reserves.

Bitget is reopening withdrawals in stages, starting with bitcoin on Monday, followed by ether and USDT. Withdrawals of other tokens, along with fiat and peer-to-peer services, are set to resume Oct 2, Bitget said in a post on its website. The staggered rollout was a security measure “unrelated to the sufficiency or availability of user assets,” the company said.

The exodus is another blow to the exchange — among the world’s top 10 by trading volume — as it seeks to recover from a hack that cybersecurity experts have said was likely linked to North Korea. Tuesday’s outflows represent more than 10% of its current reserves.

The US$464 million user protection fund Bitget had cited to assure customers their funds were safe has now fallen below US$200 million, according to the three wallet addresses that Bitget cites as the source of the funds.

See also: Bitcoin rally wobbles as macro risks overshadow ETF demand

“The Protection Fund is being used to absorb the financial impact of the incident,” Bitget CEO Gracy Chen said in an emailed response to Bloomberg. “Bitget will replenish the fund using its own capital, with the fund targeted to be above US$300 million within one week.”

Chen said she “immediately got involved with the team” after waking up around the time of the hack at 2.30am in Singapore.

See also: Crypto exchange Bitget says hackers stole US$352 mil

The attacker exploited a vulnerability in a security product supplied by a third party to obtain internal credentials, which were used to send fraudulent withdrawal commands to Bitget’s wallet system, according to Chen. Those commands bypassed existing risk controls, resulting in abnormal transfers.

The breach was confined to portions of hot-wallet and warm-wallet infrastructure, according to Chen. A subsequent investigation found that no private keys or cold wallets were compromised, she added. Hot wallets stay online for frequent transactions, cold wallets stay offline for maximum security while warm wallets sit in between.

In addition to working to replenish the funds, the exchange is working with Google’s Mandiant and blockchain-security firm SlowMist to continue to investigate the hack.

While Chen initially pointed to signs of North Korean involvement, a link that outside researchers have now also made, she was cautious about making a final conclusion at this stage.

“What I shared previously was based on preliminary indicators identified during the investigation,” she said. “Those indicators are still being assessed and should not be treated as a definitive attribution.”

title: Zheneng Jinjiang Environment to be taken private with offer of 70 cents per share
article:
A group of investors led by the largest shareholder of Zheneng Jinjiang Environment Holding Company plans to privatise the company with an offer of 70 cents per share.

The shareholder, Hong Kong listed Zhejiang Energy Hong Kong Holding, is linked to the provincial government of China's Zhejiang province, as are the other parties jointly making the offer.

The offer price of 70 cents is a premium of 19.7% over the last traded price.

Zheneng Jinjiang Environment Holding, listed on the SGX since 2016, last tapped the markets here for funding in 2018.

It has not since then and is unlikely to do so in the foreseeable future.

By taking the company private, the offeror will enjoy more flexibility to manage the business while saving on listing fees, reads the company's announcement.

title: Thailand eyes pivot to short-term debt as bond volatility rises
article:
(Sept 29): Thailand may turn to shorter-term instruments to meet the government’s borrowing needs in the fiscal year starting Oct 1, a top official said, as rising US Treasury yields drive turbulence across global bond markets.

The Public Debt Management Office is considering greater use of treasury bills, term loans and promissory notes, its director-general Jindarat Viriyataveekul told reporters in Bangkok on Tuesday. She said the agency is assessing investor demand across maturities and newly issued debt may have shorter tenors.

“This is a challenge for us, as the global market is quite volatile,” Jindarat said.

The PDMO may initially raise new funds and refinance debt using short-term instruments, then convert the borrowing into longer-term securities when market conditions become more favourable, Jindarat said. Borrowing for state-enterprise projects and programmes under emergency decrees may initially take the form of term loans or promissory notes to better match project timelines.

Thailand plans 1.26 trillion baht of new borrowing in the fiscal year 2027, with public debt projected to climb to 69.7% of gross domestic product. Jindarat said the debt ratio will likely peak in the fiscal year 2028 but remain below the 70% ceiling set under Thailand’s fiscal framework.

The impact of higher global yields on the government’s existing debt portfolio should be limited because about 89% of its borrowing is long-term, Jindarat said. That leaves refinancing and interest-rate risks largely concentrated in new debt issuance.

See also: UK set to pay highest yield since 1999 at 10-year bond auction

The government’s average borrowing cost remains about 2.6%, little changed from the previous year. Jindarat said she expects only a modest increase in the coming fiscal year because the volume of new borrowing is not excessively large.

title: Airbus freighter takes first flight to challenge Boeing’s 777
article:
(Sept 29): Airbus SE flew its new A350 freighter for the first time on Tuesday morning, an important milestone in the European planemaker’s quest to gain a bigger slice of the growing cargo business long dominated by Boeing Co.

Painted in a cardboard beige to resemble a package, the aircraft took off from Airbus’s Toulouse facility in southern France, where the company is based.

The A350 freighter was originally supposed to enter operations in 2025 but supply chain constraints caused repeated delays. The aircraft is now due to start commercial service with customers in the second half of next year.

The freighter is built using the platform of Airbus’ biggest aircraft in production, the A350-1000. It is specifically built as a freighter rather than many cargo-carrying models that have been converted from passenger aircraft.

The plane is set to compete with Boeing’s 777 and 747, which account for the bulk of global cargo operations. Airbus has received more than 100 orders for the aircraft, including 20 from Atlas Air, one of the biggest air freight operators in the world and previously a loyal Boeing customer.

Recent geopolitical woes have created an uptick in demand for transporting cargo by air to avoid risky waters like the strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, where ships have been delayed or damaged.

See also: SIA Engineering and Rolls Royce JV SAESL eyes growth as MRO market expands to US$120 bil

title: UK set to pay highest yield since 1999 at 10-year bond auction
article:
(Sept 29): The UK government is set to pay the highest yield since 1999 at an upcoming auction of 10-year debt, as investors demand additional premiums to compensate for persistent inflation and the prospect of spending increases in next month’s budget.

Britain’s Debt Management Office is scheduled to sell up to £4.25 billion (US$5.6 billion or $7.19 billion) of 4.875% coupon bonds maturing in July 2036 on Tuesday. A sale of the same security last month notched an average yield of 5.16%, already the highest in nearly two decades. Since then, 10-year yields have climbed further, hitting a 19-year peak of 5.38% on Monday. Yields stood at 5.41% on Tuesday.

The surge in gilt yields is part of the global increase in borrowing costs, as elevated energy prices fan fears that inflation will remain higher for longer, forcing central banks to tighten policy further. In addition, there are concerns over the huge scale of public borrowing and the resulting increase in the debt-servicing burden.

“Borrowing figures remain incredibly challenged, while events in the Middle East show no sign of calming and thus energy costs will remain raised,” said Richard Carter, head of fixed interest research at Quilter Cheviot Ltd. “That desire for fiscal discipline could be left wanting unless growth prospects suddenly change.”

In the UK, traders expect the Bank of England to raise interest rates in November, pricing as many as five rate hikes by end-2027.

See also: Philippines starts sale of retail bonds amid elevated rates

Meanwhile, the Oct 28 budget will be a high-stakes moment for Chancellor of the Exchequer, John Healey, who has sought to reassure investors that Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government will keep tight control of the purse strings. On Monday, he went to lengths to pledge fiscal restraint in his debut budget.

Still, higher yields are enticing some investors to buy. Last month’s 10-year auction was oversubscribed more than 3.6 times, the strongest demand since April 2020. Gilts may also get support from the BOE’s decision to pause its quantitative tightening programme and no longer sell long-dated debt into the market.

Bidding for the bond auction closes at 10am in London, with the results announced a few minutes later.

title: UK mortgage approvals fall to 32-month low as loan costs bite
article:
(Sept 29): Demand for home loans unexpectedly fell in August as higher borrowing costs triggered by the Iran war put off prospective homebuyers.

The number of mortgage approvals fell for a second consecutive month to 54,918 from a downwardly revised 55,928 in July, the Bank of England said Tuesday. It was the lowest figure since December 2023. Economists expected no change.

The report suggests that borrowing costs are taking an increasing toll, with key mortgage rates now close to 6% as the conflict in the Middle East continues. The housing market is also under pressure from growing speculation that Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey will increase property taxes in his debut budget to stabilise public finances.

Property surveyors expect house prices to fall over the next three months. London, a market that’s especially vulnerable to potential levies on high-value homes, is looking particularly weak. Official figures showed average house prices in the capital declined by around £20,000 from their peak in mid-2025.

“Many prospective buyers have understandably been taking a more cautious approach and waiting to see what measures are announced in the Autumn Budget,” said Nathan Emerson, CEO at Propertymark.

See also: Burnham’s vision for Britain puts pensions ‘triple lock’ in play

Healey faces a tough balancing act between easing investors' worries around the UK’s growing debt pile and supporting households with the cost of living. The government has said it wants to introduce a new loan scheme to help first-time buyers purchase new-build homes, as it tries to sustain some of the confidence boost it delivered over the summer.

The Bank of England is expected to provide limited support going forward. Rate-setters have warned that an increase in interest rates is becoming more likely the longer the war in Iran continues, as elevated energy prices risk spreading across the economy.

While homebuyer demand is weakening, consumers have been relatively resilient since the start of the Iran war. Cushioned by a healthy savings buffer, households have been saving less and borrowing more to spend their way through the energy price shock.

See also: Burnham signals reluctance to raise taxes in UK budget

The latest BOE figures showed consumers borrowed an extra £2.5 billion in August, up from £2.1 billion in July and well above the six-month average of £1.9 billion. Net borrowing on credit cards rose to £1.2 billion from £900 million. Other forms of credit, such as car dealership finance and personal loans, also increased.

“The rise in borrowing comes alongside a two-year high in consumer confidence, driven by a better outlook for personal finances and economic conditions,” Katie Clinton, head of financial services advisory at KPMG UK, said. However, she added that the figures also reflect more people taking credit “to get by".

“With inflation expected to rise in the coming months and as households head towards the traditionally busy pre-Christmas spending period, pressure on budgets could intensify,” Clinton added.

title: Burnham’s vision for Britain puts pensions ‘triple lock’ in play
article:
(Sept 29): UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham will pitch for honest political debate as the antidote to populism, as he reveals his plans for taking on thorny issues at his party’s annual conference.

He’ll say that involves spending money to address a crisis in Britain’s social care system, raising the prospect that he could pay for it by taking on the totemic triple lock that protects pension increases.

In his first speech as the prime minister to the governing Labour Party’s gathering in Liverpool, Burnham will make clear his willingness to take on the challenges he will argue predecessors have ducked, including plans to tackle rising youth unemployment and fix a crisis-hit care system. He’ll pledge to end the “drift” of recent years by providing more “direction” to the country.

Labour officials expect Burnham could signal he wants to begin a national conversation about reforming the state pension to help pay for social care. Many economists say the country’s so-called triple lock, which guarantees that the state pension rises by the highest of inflation, wage growth or 2.5%, is unaffordable.

No major political party has yet been willing to propose dropping the commitment, fearful of antagonising Britain’s older population. Ministers have also signalled this week that Labour’s longer-term ambitions are unlikely to be affordable without tax rises.

A Labour spokesperson declined to answer questions about whether the party would change the triple lock, saying only that the party was committed to keeping it until the next general election.

See also: Burnham signals reluctance to raise taxes in UK budget

UK gilts opened higher on Tuesday, outperforming European and US counterparts, in a move driven by lower energy prices. Benchmark 10-year UK yields fell five basis points to 5.37%.

There was limited reaction to overnight reports on Burnham’s speech. However UK swap spreads, which measure the difference between 30-year UK government bond yields and risk-free rates and act as a proxy for sentiment about UK fiscal risk, have narrowed slightly.

By turning to meaty and long-standing issues, Burnham is seeking to counter criticism from opposition parties that he’s relied on announcing relatively cheap, feel-good measures to lift sentiment during his first two months in office. The challenge is that the larger policies come with a price tag, and bond investors will be watching closely for any new spending that could increase the country’s debt burden.

See also: Burnham stands by remarks that UK is in hock to bond markets

Burnham will tell delegates in Liverpool: “We can’t carry on as we are,” according to remarks briefed in advance by his office. “Politics-as-usual has taken Britain backwards. More of the same isn’t good enough and isn’t going to get us where we need to be.”

Some in Labour are nonetheless wary of the political risk of going into a general election, which Burnham has said will take place in 2029, pledging to dent pensioners’ income and raise taxes. Sharon Graham, the general secretary of the Unite trade union, told the BBC it would be “morally wrong” to end the triple lock and that doing so would be “electoral suicide”.

The start of Labour’s four-day conference in Liverpool was dominated by Burnham’s promise to revamp the care system for the elderly and infirm to make it universally free at the point of use, like Britain’s National Health Service. While he has hinted at new taxes to pay for the policy he has not yet set out what form these will take, prompting accusations from opposition parties he has no concrete plan to pay for it. Reforming the triple lock could get him part of the way there.

Burnham on Sunday promised to outline his planned overhaul of the system and put it to the public in a vote at the next general election, due in 2029. Pressed on how it would be funded, Burnham told LBC a day later: “I will reveal detail tomorrow.”

He said he couldn’t move faster because of the constraints imposed by Labour’s 2024 election manifesto, which pledged not to put up three key levels of tax, the Treasury’s biggest revenue raisers. He also said it “will take time, I’m afraid, to get the detail right.”

As well as social care, Burnham’s office promised “a raft of policies and commitments” in his speech, including on energy, water and housing. There was little detail beyond that, but there have been hints in recent days, with the prime minister saying last week that he would lay out a plan to reset the water industry — a sector he has repeatedly hinted should be under public control.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

The Labour government will offer “a more serious prospectus for Britain than people have been offered in a generation”, the prime minister will say. “I accept people will not agree with every part of it, but I believe it can turn Britain around.”

Social care is probably the thorniest issue Burnham is seeking to resolve. He tried to take it on as the health secretary 17 years ago, with a plan to tax estates after people had died. That was branded a death tax by Conservatives. The Tories in 2017 attempted reforms of their own that were branded a dementia tax.

“This has been highly contentious: all parties have used this for point-scoring purposes, dementia tax, death tax, you name it,” he said in the interview. “The problem with that is, it’s put politics before people, and that’s why it’s been unreformed for all of these years.”

Also on the prime minister’s to-do list is tackling the country’s youth unemployment crisis, with the out-of-work rate among 16 to 24-year-olds at 16.4%, the highest since 2014.

A review into the issue by former Labour health secretary Alan Milburn is due for publication imminently, and Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden hinted on Sunday that it would make recommendations around tightening the criteria on benefit eligibility. That in turn would help to bear down on another pressing issue, Britain’s soaring benefits bill.

Another announcement planned by Burnham will be to establish a public body called Great British Grid to work with private electricity network companies in order to speed up grid connections. The government said it would expand the rights of businesses to build connection infrastructure themselves, with the option of co-investment from the new organisation.

Burnham will also lay out proposals to deliver on a pledge of asserting more public control over the country’s water industry, which has been plagued by leaks and sewage spills in recent years. Last week he promised his speech would contain details of the planned reset, saying “privatisation has failed and people can see that very clearly in relation to water”.

Britain is currently “run for vested interests, not in the public interest, with power held in too few hands”, Burnham will say on Tuesday, according to his office. The country needs “more control of the basics so that we can make it more functional again”, he’ll add. He’ll also reiterate his view that successive governments have pursued “flawed thinking of the last 40 years”.

“Everyone wants less drift and more direction,” the prime minister will say, pledging to “answer that call”. “Hope comes from honesty and from saying the things politicians usually avoid.”

title: China said to offer cheap loans to help state firms pay overdue bills
article:
(Sept 29): China has started offering low-cost funding to help local government-affiliated firms settle unpaid bills, according to people familiar with the matter, expanding efforts to mend corporate balance sheets and remove one of the biggest bottlenecks for investment.

The People’s Bank of China (PBOC) set up a new relending facility to provide cheap capital to commercial and policy banks, they said, asking not to be identified discussing a decision that hasn’t been made public. The goal is to encourage the lenders to extend credit to mostly state-owned companies known as local government financing vehicles, or LGFVs, and other firms linked to local authorities, according to the people.

The central bank is setting no quota and will instead disburse funds as needed, they added, in a departure from its other so-called structural tools that cap the amount available to eligible financial institutions. Banks can already apply for the funding from the PBOC, which has made no official announcement about the facility and doesn’t list it among its other targeted lending programmes.

Estimates vary about how much is at stake. Researchers at China Chengxin International Credit Rating Co, one of the country’s largest rating firms, said last year that local governments and their affiliates had 4.5 trillion yuan (US$670 billion or $858 billion) of overdue payments, equivalent to more than 3% of China’s gross domestic product.

The novel source of financing means a bigger role for the PBOC in working through the backlog of arrears that’s cascaded through the economy, putting the squeeze on corporate cash flow and damaging trust in business dealings with the government. It’s also a sign of closer coordination between fiscal and monetary policy in supporting the economy that needs to unlock investment after an intensifying slowdown.

The PBOC didn’t immediately respond to a Bloomberg request for comments.

See also: China broadens travel curbs to encompass family of top AI talent

The programme is designed to help companies make overdue payments owed to contractors and suppliers, the people said. The arrangement, details of which haven’t previously been reported, merited a brief mention in a statement made in August by the State Council, China’s Cabinet headed by Premier Li Qiang.

Without elaborating, it revealed that local authorities could tap a targeted relending facility as the government vowed to “accelerate and intensify” the campaign to clear arrears owed to companies. Coming a month after the Communist Party’s powerful Politburo called on officials to address the problem “on a regular basis”, it marked the latest government push to boost business confidence as China’s unprecedented investment slump worsens.

See also: China’s consumer stocks face lost decade as AI steals spotlight

After shrinking in 2025 for the first time in data going back almost three decades, fixed-asset investment fell 7.2% from a year earlier in the first eight months of 2026. The drop-off in private capital spending was even worse, with a slump of over 10% in January-August leaving it on track for its fourth straight year of decline.

Payments in arrears have soared as a years-long housing downturn and slowing growth dented local government income and cut into the cash flow of property developers.

Nomura Holdings Inc has argued that developers are at the center of China’s complicated inter-firm debt network, estimating they alone had around 7.8 trillion yuan in overdue payments.

The delinquent debt is adding to pressure on companies already having to navigate the challenges posed by excess capacity and fierce competition with rivals. That’s thinned profit margins and trapped working capital while further undermining the confidence and willingness of businesses to invest.

Wu Zhiwu, a senior research and development director at CSCI Pengyuan Credit Ratings, wrote in a report last October that the authorities identified 1.8 trillion yuan in arrears owed by self-funded and partially government-backed public institutions, local state-owned enterprises and LGFVs, with a plan to see the debt resolved by providing specialised bank loans.

Proceeds from local bond sales would go towards covering past-due payments of regional governments and fully state-backed public institutions, for which no official tally was available, Wu said. Local administrations had no less than 2.8 trillion yuan in arrears for construction projects as of end-2024, he estimated.

Nomura economists including Lu Ting said in a report earlier this month that “the key to rejuvenating China’s economy” is in clearing out the backlog.

“Given the unique systemic importance of trade credit and the severity of current inter-firm arrears, we strongly believe that cleaning up these arrears is the prerequisite for a genuine recovery in China’s domestic demand and the stabilisation of the property sector,” they said.

title: Shein sinks 14% after operating profit plunge in debut earnings
article:
(Sept 29): Shares of Shein Global Holdings Ltd fell as much as 14% after the online fashion retailer reported a 53% plunge in first-half operating income in its inaugural earnings as a public company.

The drop was Shein’s biggest since its Hong Kong debut on Sept 1, capping US$10 billion lost in market value since it started trading at a valuation of roughly US$26 billion.

Rising costs and weakening demand have squeezed Shein’s margins, with the pressure intensifying in the second quarter, the Singapore-based fast-fashion company said Monday. Shein cited higher freight costs driven by an increase in oil prices amid conflict in the Middle East while growth in its core retail business has also slowed.

“We expect the external environment to remain uncertain in the second half of 2026, with tariff headwinds and logistics cost volatility likely to persist,” Shein CEO Sky Xu said in a statement.

Xu also pointed to a tougher consumer landscape, saying shoppers were grappling with higher inflation and becoming selective about purchases.

That pullback appears to extend beyond Shein. Two of its suppliers interviewed by Bloomberg said their business with PDD Holdings Inc’s Temu has also weakened while the rival platform’s global web traffic has fallen since March. Time spent on Temu and Amazon.com Inc also declined this summer.

See also: China said to offer cheap loans to help state firms pay overdue bills

Shein’s sales have underperformed the broader apparel industry in the US since late last year. Rivals including PDD Holdings Inc’s Temu and Amazon.com Inc have posted single- to double-digit growth since April.

Jefferies said earnings estimates for Shein in 2026 and 2027 may be too optimistic as margins will face growing pressure with the European Union eliminating a customs exemption on low-value parcels in July. Second-quarter’s adjusted profit “likely missed consensus by a wide margin", analysts including John Chou wrote in a note Tuesday.

Early indicators suggest the business pressure for Shein is continuing into the third quarter. US sales fell more than 10% in the three months through August, according to Bloomberg Second Measure, which analyses credit and debit card transactions.

title: Spanish inflation unexpectedly hits 5%, backing higher rates
article:
(Sept 29): Spanish inflation accelerated more than anticipated and further beyond the European Central Bank’s 2% target, reinforcing the case for interest rates to be lifted further.

Consumer prices jumped 5% in September, up from 4.6% in August, data Tuesday showed. That is the highest since February 2023 and above the 4.9% median estimate in a Bloomberg survey of analysts.

Fuel and package holidays were behind the steep rise, the statistics agency said. A gauge of underlying price pressures also advanced more than expected.

Europe is grappling with a renewed upswing in energy costs stemming from the Iran war, though the region’s economy has so far held up surprisingly well. Spain’s numbers are the first for this month from a major euro-area member and are likely to be the highest. While others will also probably report faster readings, they should all come in below 4%.

Eurostat will release figures on Friday for the 21-nation euro zone. Economists estimate inflation reached a three-year high of 3.7%.

See also: European stocks advance as UK homebuilders rally; miners drop

That is unlikely to be the peak, however. A monthly sentiment poll by the European Commission found firms’ selling-price expectations held above long-term averages in all sectors while consumers’ inflation expectations for the next 12 months rose "noticeably".

A national gauge of price increases in Belgium, meanwhile, neared 5% in September, separate data Tuesday showed.

Speaking on Monday, ECB President Christine Lagarde reiterated that second-round inflation effects are so far absent, meaning the ECB should adopt a “measured response as appropriate to keep inflation in check”.

See also: Eurozone business activity hits three-year high on services

While policymakers have so far raised the deposit rate twice, to 2.5%, markets are pricing almost four more quarter-point moves in this cycle. Traders trimmed bets after Lagarde said higher bond yields will weigh on inflation as well as the economy.

Spain has been the continent’s standout growth story, contributing to its speedier inflation. Gross domestic product will rise 2.3% this year and 1.7% in 2027, according to the country’s central bank, while unemployment is at the lowest since the financial crisis in 2008.

Inflation for the whole of 2026 is likely to come in at 3.6%, the Bank of Spain said in June, before the latest surge in oil and natural gas prices.

title: Asia may weather tight global diesel market better than Europe — Bloomberg analysis
article:
(Sept 29): Asia looks to be better positioned than Europe to weather an emerging global diesel crunch, with the Trump administration weighing export curbs that could tighten supplies of the key fuel even further.

Spot cargoes delivered into Northwest Europe are increasingly more expensive than in the main Asian refining and trading hub of Singapore, according to a Bloomberg analysis of General Index data. The widening differential — which averaged about US$174 a ton so far in September, from US$27 in May — reflects the relative strength of the two markets, and takes freight into account.

The global market for diesel — used to power trucking, farm equipment and industry — is acutely tight following seven months of war in the Middle East, as well as a prolonged shipment ban imposed by Russia after waves of Ukrainian drone attacks on refineries. With pump costs hitting records in America, President Donald Trump has mulled a ban on US exports, with analysts warning that such a move could supercharge overseas prices, especially in Europe.

Refiners across Asia have already been able to secure much of their crude oil feedstock for the coming months, so they’ll be able to keep making fuels even with continued disruptions to shipping in the Persian Gulf. Among producers, India has said it intends to keep honoring overseas contracts for diesel, while China — typically a major exporter — has eased curbs on flows seen earlier in the conflict. Elsewhere, Japan’s exports may also rebound.

“Based on current refining operating rates and crude availability, there are no major issues with diesel supply in Asia,” said June Goh, senior oil market analyst at Sparta Commodities SA. “In fact, the likelihood is for Asia supporting Europe with diesel exports if Trump really bans US exports.”

See also: Oil extends gain as Iran uncertainty outweighs Saudi pipe return

title: Demand boost for US crops still unclear after China tariff cuts
article:
(Sept 29): A day after China announced tariff cuts across a slew of US agricultural products, crop traders are trying to parse whether — and how quickly — that will translate into a demand pickup for major grains.

Soybeans were excluded from the reductions and sluggish economic growth has sapped Chinese demand for corn and wheat imports. The timing of the levy cuts also remains unclear, with both countries first required to complete procedures required under domestic law.

That’s keeping prices for grains subdued. Soybean futures edged lower in Chicago after dropping more than 2% on Monday. Wheat and corn also fell further after declining in the previous session.

“China’s decision to keep the 10% tariff on US soybeans reflects its desire to maintain flexibility in managing imported soybean supplies,” said Liu Haowen, an analyst at Wuchan Zhongda Futures Co.

China is set to reduce duties on US wheat, corn and sorghum, according to lists released by the two countries on Monday. The cuts are part of a plan to lower tariffs on about US$30 billion of imports from each side, following last week’s summit between the leaders of the two nations.

The American Soybean Association said in a statement that it was “disappointed” that US beans weren’t included among the tariff cuts, and urged trade negotiators to pursue a trade deal that provides additional support for American supplies.

See also: World’s top coal exporter strains to lift output as prices soar

China’s annual commitment provides “critical stability, and we expect those commitments to be fully met,” said Scott Metzger, the association’s president and an Ohio soybean farmer.

That leaves the market counting on previous Chinese pledges to buy more US farm products. Beijing committed to buy at least 25 million tonnes of US soybeans annually through 2028 and, in addition, at least US$17 billion of American agricultural products.

State-owned firms Cofco and Sinograin have been making steady progress on buying US soybeans, helping Beijing meet more than half of the target for this year. Sinograin has also been selling beans from reserves, a move seen as making space for incoming American shipments.

See also: Copper slides as China industrial data weighs on demand outlook

On the US$17-billion pledge, China still has a significant amount of buying to do with just over three months to go, Wuchan Zhongda’s Liu said.

title: Philippines starts sale of retail bonds amid elevated rates
article:
(Sept 29): The Philippines raised 84.9 billion pesos in a retail Treasury bond auction, securing fresh funds for government spending while opting for a shorter tenor amid elevated interest rates.

The 2.5-year bonds due 2029 fetched a coupon of 6.875% at the price-setting auction Tuesday, with bids totalling 188.6 billion pesos. The coupon rate is comparable to the 6.865% yield on the existing 2.5-year government bond based on the Bloomberg evaluated pricing service BVAL.

The government will offer the bonds to the public through Oct 7, and existing holders may exchange notes due this and next year for the new securities.

Bond sales to retail investors are a big source of financing for the Philippine government, making up a significant share of its annual borrowings. Other countries across Asia, including Indonesia and India, are also broadening retail access to such debt to diversify their investor base beyond institutional and foreign holders.

Retail bonds in the Philippines are typically offered in smaller denominations of 5,000 pesos, making them accessible to a large base of savers seeking higher returns than bank deposits. They have generally been well received, with the issuance in August 2025 raising 507.2 billion pesos after a record sale of 585 billion pesos in February 2024.

The decision to issue a shorter tenor is a strategic move, National Treasurer Sharon Almanza said at a media briefing.

See also: Paramount puts US$44 bil bond sale for Warner deal in motion

“Given where the rates are and how defensive the market is, we also want to make sure that we are not adding costs for the government,” she said. “We’re still hoping that by next year, rates will moderate. So definitely, we don’t want to lock in at a very high rate.”

Borrowing funds from retail investors, a programme first introduced in 2001, could reduce the borrowing costs for Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr’s administration at a time when high inflation and a selloff in the global debt market have sent rates soaring. The central bank has signalled further interest-rate hikes to contain inflation which has accelerated as the peso falls and oil prices rise.

The government plans to borrow a total of 2.73 trillion pesos this year before raising another 3.3 trillion pesos in 2027.

See also: Bond market is getting closer to sounding alarm on US economy

The government aims to raise 150 billion pesos in new money from the current borrowing exercise and expects an additional amount from the bond exchange, Almanza said. The funds will help finance various government projects, including agriculture, education, healthcare and infrastructure, according to the treasury bureau.

title: China offers mortgage subsidies to boost ailing property sector
article:
(Sept 29): China will subsidise mortgage interest payments for first-time homebuyers nationwide, as policymakers step up efforts to revive the housing market amid a prolonged property downturn and slowing economic growth.

First-home buyers will get subsidies worth an annualised rate of one percentage point of the mortgage principal, according to a Ministry of Finance statement late Tuesday. To qualify, homes must be 120 square meters or smaller and priced at 1.5 million yuan (US$224,000 or $286,481) or less.

China’s years-long housing slump, with new-home prices falling for more than three years straight, has been a major drag on the economy. The country’s growth has likely weakened further below the bottom end of the government’s annual target in the third quarter after reaching 4.3% in the previous three months, with consumption flatlining and investment falling into a deeper slump.

In late September, China’s cabinet promised to introduce new measures to support the economy and study policies to stabilise the reeling property market, saying it will “put in place a package of practical and effective additional policies” to safeguard this year’s economic goals.

title: Bangkok floods hit Thai Airways, Honda as disruption spreads
article:
(Sept 29): Thailand stepped up relief efforts as severe flooding spread disruption from Bangkok’s streets to airline schedules and auto production, widening the economic toll from days of torrential rain.

The cabinet has approved about four billion baht (US$119 million or $150 million) in flood relief, Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said Tuesday. Authorities are also working to drain inundated neighbourhoods and deliver supplies to stranded residents.

The disruption has spread to major industries. Thai Airways International Pcl cancelled 22 domestic and international flights scheduled for Sept 29-30 after flooding prevented many employees from reaching work, triggering flight delays and leaving more than 5,000 bags stranded at Bangkok’s Suvarnabhumi Airport.

The flag carrier has cut capacity by about 30% from roughly 110 daily departures from Bangkok to stabilise its remaining operations. Chief executive officer Chai Eamsiri expects services to return to normal within 72 hours and apologised to affected passengers. The company’s shares declined as much as 2.4%.

Tourism and Sports Minister Surasak Phancharoenworakul said Thai Airways’ handling of the disruption had hurt Thailand’s tourism image and called on the Finance Ministry, its largest shareholder, to convene an urgent board meeting.

Authorities are closely watching Prachin Buri and Rayong, part of Thailand’s eastern industrial belt and a major centre for auto manufacturing. Water levels in Prachin Buri may begin receding, while Rayong faces further heavy rain and water releases from spillways, government spokesman Ekkapob Pianpises said at an emergency briefing Tuesday.

See also: Singapore’s annual growth rate to stabilise at 2.7% for the next decade, amid wider divergence in Southeast Asia

Honda Motor Co suspended motorcycle production at one of its Thai plants on Monday and Tuesday because of flooding, a company official said, confirming an earlier Nikkei Asia report. The plant is expected to resume operations Wednesday.

The wider auto industry has so far avoided significant disruption, with most factories operating and parts shipments largely unaffected, according to the Federation of Thai Industries. The group maintained its 2026 production target of 1.45 million vehicles.

The floods have also disrupted 155 schools in Bangkok, some of which have been inundated for four or five days, Education Minister Prasert Jantararuangtong said. Some won’t reopen this week, examinations have been postponed and campuses are being used as evacuation centres.

See also: Philippines’ ombudsman files plunder case against Marcos cousin

The disruption follows a deluge that dumped more than 12 inches of rain on Bangkok over two to three days, nearly as much as the capital typically receives during the entire month of September. Drainage systems were overwhelmed, leaving roads and homes submerged.

As of Sept 28, flooding had affected 1,267 businesses across 40 provinces, including 52 factories and 1,162 small and medium-sized enterprises. Preliminary damage was estimated at 22.2 million baht.

The same weather system also brought severe flooding to neighbouring Myanmar, where heavy rain and runoff inundated more than 40 villages in the southern Tanintharyi region. At least one person was confirmed dead and more than 8,000 people were displaced in Dawei district, according to Myanmar’s Ministry of Social Welfare, Relief and Resettlement.

The mounting damage in Thailand is adding urgency to longer-term flood defences.

The cabinet is also considering a 160 billion-baht, eight-year project to divert floodwater from northern Thailand away from heavily populated areas downstream, according to Danucha Pichayanan, secretary-general of the National Economic and Social Development Council.

Some funding has already been allocated, while additional borrowing may be used to speed construction, he said.

title: Lindt to cut prices as chocolate demand wanes in key markets
article:
(Sept 29): Lindt plans to lower prices for its chocolate products after it pared back its sales-growth guidance for a second time this year citing subdued consumer sentiment.

The Swiss company is cutting prices for its Christmas offerings and plans to lower them across the board starting in January, CEO Adalbert Lechner said Tuesday on a media call. Lindt earlier revised its full-year 2026 outlook for organic sales growth to a range of 0%–2%, down from 4–6% previously, having already trimmed it in March.

The shares slumped as much as 8.7% in Zurich, the biggest intraday decline since the March guidance revision. They were down by more than a quarter this year through Monday’s close due to doubts about a recovery in volumes.

The confectionary maker has been grappling with tepid demand in Germany, Switzerland and Austria, as well as increased price sensitivity among customers. A heat wave also weighed on sales in Europe across the chocolate industry during the summer months.

“A second cut within six months dents Lindt’s reputation for reliable guidance, a key support for its premium valuation,” Vontobel analyst Jean-Philippe Bertschy wrote in a note. “Pricing power, long Lindt’s trump card, is now being tested.”

Record-high cocoa prices have been another factor holding back profitability at chocolatiers in recent years. They started to come down toward the second half of 2025 but have been on the rise again since February on expectations that West Africa’s 2026-27 crop will be smaller because of disease and adverse weather.

See also: Jollibee cuts store, spending targets as cost pressures linger

The region could also be affected by a strong El Niño, a climate phenomenon which can bring periods of severe flooding or drought. Lindt and its rivals are usually hedged well into the future and may have to wait before reaping the benefits of any price normalisation.

Swiss cocoa grinder Barry Callebaut AG has reported lower volumes due to higher market prices. While it flagged an improvement in orders in its third-quarter results, with customers willing to book further in advance again, it warned that recovery “would take some time".

Lindt, or Chocoladefabriken Lindt & Spruengli AG, expects “positive volume growth” next year thanks to an easing cocoa market and increased brand investments, Lechner said.

See also: Thailand approves US$688 mil investment by Nestle for smart factory, distribution centre

“With our hedging strategy, we did not benefit in a big way from lower cocoa prices this year but we will see a positive impact next year that allows us to do lower price points,” he told reporters.

Lower prices introduced in August in some of its key markets had already shown “that there is a direct link to volume development", he added.

Lindt’s premium positioning has been flagged as a possible hurdle to volume recovery by analysts, as consumers who opted for cheaper alternatives could take longer to return.

“We have quite a few opportunities to continue to grow volume because we believe that the trend to premiumisation as an overall trend will continue,” Lechner said.

title: Australia raises key rate to 15-year high to cool inflation
article:
(Sept 29): Australia’s central bank resumed raising interest rates on Tuesday, judging it couldn’t wait any longer to respond to rising energy costs and resilient domestic demand that threaten to intensify inflationary pressures.

The Reserve Bank’s board lifted the cash rate to 4.6% from 4.35%, as widely expected, taking rates to the highest level in about 15 years. The nine-member policy committee voted unanimously to deliver its fourth hike this year, saying firms are experiencing cost pressures and either increasing prices or looking to do so.

“Since the previous meeting, some of the upside risks to inflation are materialising,” the policy board said in its statement. “The board will continue to do what it considers necessary to bring inflation sustainably back to target, including increasing the cash rate target further if needed.”

The Australian dollar fluctuated between a small gain and loss to hold above 70 US cents as investors digested the decision. Yields on policy-sensitive three-year notes trimmed an earlier decline to trade one basis point lower at 5.03%.

Traders lifted bets on a further RBA rate hike, with swaps pricing a 56% chance of a follow-up move in November. Prior to the decision, it was seen as roughly a coin toss.

See also: South Korea tax windfall seen above 50 tril won — Yonhap

The RBA joins counterparts in Europe, the US and Japan in raising rates this month to tackle escalating price pressures fueled by the US-Iran war. With little prospect of an early resolution to the conflict and energy prices surging across the global economy, central banks are having to act.

“November’s RBA meeting is live, particularly given today’s unanimous decision,” Katherine Palmer, head of fixed income strategy at BlackRock’s Australian unit wrote in a note. “Domestic capacity pressures continue, while elevated oil prices and geopolitical uncertainty have added to the risk that inflation remains persistent.”

RBA officials had sent increasingly hawkish signals in recent weeks and indicated a willingness to hike if needed to try to ensure inflation heads back to its 2%-3% target band. The central bank increased borrowing costs at its first three meetings of the year, worrying about building price pressures even before the energy shock unleashed by war in the Middle East.

See also: It’s time to reconsider inflation targeting

“Higher fuel prices have partially been passed through to prices of other goods and services. This inflation impulse is in addition to the effect of capacity pressures in the economy,” the statement said. “The board remains focused on ensuring that high inflation does not become embedded.”

The RBA stood pat at 4.35% at its past two meetings, trying to gauge the impact of its rapid-fire moves on the economy. Tuesday’s hike now takes cumulative tightening this year to 1 percentage point. The risk of a follow-up rate rise in November has also been widely discussed by economists due to the spectre of price pressures becoming entrenched.

The OECD has projected that inflation in wealthy nations will linger in 2027, warning central banks including Australia’s to “remain very vigilant” and intervene more than they did during the post-pandemic period. The International Monetary Fund sent a similar warning to the RBA directly this month, urging it to stand ready to hike.

Australia will release monthly inflation data for August on Wednesday, which is likely to be an important input for policymakers, though the RBA’s favoured quarterly report will be available before the next meeting in November.

The statement “delivers a consistent message of inflation concern, despite the three prior rate hikes, the slowdown in housing, and the slight easing in labour market strength”, said Sean Keane, chief strategist for Asia Pacific at JB Drax Honore. “This is a central bank that is clearly prepared to hike again this year, not because they want to, but quite simply because they may have to.”

Tuesday’s tightening is set to weigh further on Australia’s housing market, already in a downturn and with linkages across the economy. It may push unemployment higher after the jobless rate rose to 4.6% last month.

“In Australia, weak productivity growth continues to constrain potential growth and there are uncertainties about the economic effects of the downturn in the housing market,” the board said.

title: Toyota sales fall for seventh straight month on China slump
article:
(Sept 29): Toyota Motor Corp’s car sales fell again last month due to a prolonged slump in China, where legacy brands are grappling with mounting competition from fast-moving local electric-vehicle makers.

Toyota and Lexus brand sales cratered 23% in the world’s biggest auto market in August on weak demand for gasoline and hybrid vehicles, the Japanese manufacturer said Tuesday. That dragged down its global group deliveries, which declined 7.5% from a year earlier.

Toyota and its peers have been contending with a shrinking market in China, where consumers are shying away from expensive purchases due to an ongoing real estate crisis. Carmakers are also dealing with uneven demand for EVs, and soaring oil prices triggered by the fighting in the Middle East.

Honda Motor Co’s global sales fell 9.2% in August, dragged down by a 50% slump in China. Nissan Motor Co’s deliveries in the country plummeted 52%, resulting in a global sales decline of 17.5%.

Toyota and Lexus did better elsewhere, with sales rising 2.6% in Europe and 9.1% in Japan thanks to robust demand for new models, especially hybrids. They declined 4.4% in the US and fell by more than a third in the Middle East.

Earlier this year, Toyota said hybrid sales are on track to exceed five million units for the first time in 2026. Alternative powertrains have provided the Japanese carmaker with a strong arsenal in the US, where steep tariffs have all but blocked BYD Co and other Chinese brands from entering the market.

See also: Goldman's John Waldron edges closer to succeeding Solomon as CEO

title: AMD to buy Fei-Fei Li’s World Labs AI startup for US$8.2 bil
article:
(Sept 29): Chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices Inc agreed to acquire World Labs for US$8.2 billion ($10.48 billion), gaining an artificial intelligence (AI) startup founded by industry pioneer and researcher Fei-Fei Li.

The all-stock transaction is expected to close by the end of the year, subject to regulatory approvals, the companies said in a statement Monday.

AMD, a key challenger to Nvidia Corp in the market for AI chips, is adding a team of leading researchers and their models, along with insights into how the AI field is evolving. That should help the company plan its future hardware releases.

“The more you understand end to end, the better system you are going to build,” AMD chief executive officer Lisa Su said in a Bloomberg Television interview that’s slated to air on Monday afternoon.

“That’s why we are acquiring World Labs,” Su said. “To have access to the world-class talent Fei-Fei has brought together and bring it together with AMD’s capabilities around hardware, software and systems.”

World Labs develops so-called world models: AI software that can run applications in the physical world. The models generate and reconstruct three-dimensional environments, which the startup says can be used to help advance work on robots, scientific discovery and factory equipment.

See also: China may let Alibaba buy Nvidia’s RTX chips, Information reports

Li, who served as CEO of World Labs, is a renowned researcher and computer scientist at Stanford University. As part of the agreement, she will join AMD as an executive vice president and chief scientist and report directly to Su.

“As our company grows, so does our ambition,” Li said in the Bloomberg Television interview. And that has increased the startup’s need for computing power, she said.

“At this point, if we can join forces with AMD, we really are giving ourselves, AMD and the ecosystem an opportunity to accelerate the flywheel between software and hardware development,” she said.

See also: Bill Gates says Trump is wrong to hold out against AI safeguards

The deal will also help bolster AMD’s offerings by allowing it to provide a variety of AI models to customers. The company has been expanding its lineup in a bid to sell more products and services to data centre clients, its biggest source of revenue. The idea is to offer the necessary elements to rapidly set up the facilities and put them into operation.

“You are going to have both open as well as proprietary models,” Su said. “AMD has been a contributor there. I think we are going to expand that contribution.”

Ultimately, the goal is to build better AI, Su added. “Our ambition is to define the future of AI compute.”

AMD’s larger rival Nvidia pioneered the approach of bundling equipment and services with AI chips to help clients get up and running quickly. It’s now using the strategy to target new kinds of customers — going beyond the cloud computing giants that still fuel much of its growth.

Nvidia recently agreed to acquire another high-profile AI startup, Hugging Face, in a deal valued at about US$13 billion.

World Labs, launched in 2024, has about 70 employees. That includes a team of robotics experts from its July acquisition of SceniX, a startup that builds software to train robots in realistic virtual worlds.

During Su’s 12-year tenure as AMD’s leader, the chipmaker has sought to be recognised for its technical capabilities and escape its reputation as an also-ran in Silicon Valley. In the company’s core processor market, AMD has already emerged from the shadow of Intel Corp and now has products that are rated the best in the industry.

In the market for AI accelerators — chips used to train and run AI models — AMD remains a distant second to Nvidia. But Su has rolled out new products that she says can outperform offerings from its larger rival.

Investors see the company as a key beneficiary of AI spending and have bid up its shares nearly threefold this year. That’s given AMD a valuation of roughly US$1 trillion, a distinction shared with only about a dozen other tech titans.

Nvidia remains the world’s most valuable company, with a market capitalisation above US$5 trillion. But its shares are only up about 22% this year, underperforming nearly all major chipmakers in 2026.

title: AI faces US$6 tril test to justify data centres, Bain says
article:
(Sept 29): The global AI industry needs to earn US$6 trillion in annual revenue by 2031 to justify the capital being deployed to build data centres around the world, Bain & Co said.

Existing consumer and enterprise AI services may generate as much as US$1.8 trillion of that sum, leaving US$4.2 trillion in new revenue that needs to be created, the consulting firm said Tuesday in its annual global technology report. The shortfall likely will come from nascent segments ranging from autonomous machines to robotics, as well as emerging fields such as drug discovery, mental health and energy generation, it said.

“What the industry needs is a wave of innovation that will dwarf what mobile and cloud unlocked,” said David Crawford, the report’s lead author and chairman of Bain’s Global Technology, Media, and Telecommunications practice. “AI infrastructure is being built well ahead of the demand curve and funding it sustainably will require adding approximately 1% to the annual global GDP growth rate,” he said.

Bain’s report highlights the hurdles ahead to make the current pace of AI development sustainable.

Companies led by Microsoft Corp, Alphabet Inc’s Google, Amazon.com Inc, Meta Platforms Inc and Oracle Corp are investing trillions of dollars in data centres to quench AI’s demand for computational resources. Data centre sizes and costs are doubling roughly every 12 to 16 months, in part due to surging prices of chips from the likes of Nvidia Corp and SK Hynix Inc, networking equipment and other components.

The report comes as debate intensifies around the as-yet elusive returns for AI service providers. Critics worry about an increasingly interconnected web of dependencies between technology manufacturers and AI developers that help to propel lofty expectations that in turn require bigger sums of money.

See also: Sony to skip CES show after Honda EV venture dropped

While discussions today are fixated on employee productivity, the economics of AI infrastructure will demand trillions in new revenue beyond productivity gains, Bain said.

The consultancy projects US$5 trillion to US$6.5 trillion of data-centre spending by 2030, adding at least 150 gigawatts of capacity that will further strain countries’ energy resources. Annual spending on AI infrastructure — spanning data centres, computing capacity and upgrades in accelerators and memory chips — may reach as much as US$1.5 trillion by 2031, it said.

Data center developers already face shortages in transformers and water and power supplies, as well as fierce local opposition that’s blocked or delayed US$68 billion worth of projects in the June quarter in the US.

title: MAS places $1.45 bil with five asset managers; reviewing proposals for a fourth batch of asset managers
article:
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has announced the appointment of the third batch of five asset managers under the $6.5 billion Equity Market Development Programme (EQDP).

MAS will be placing a total of $1.45 billion with five appointed managers, which are, Amundi, Franklin Templeton, HSBC Asset Management, M&G Investments and Natixis Investment Managers.

With this latest $1.45 billion allocation, this will bring the total allocation under the EQDP to $5.4 billion.

These announcements were made during the SuperReturn Asia Conference on Sept 29 by Chee Hong Tat, Minister for National Development and Deputy Chairman of MAS.

"This third batch will further deepen investment capabilities and support the creation of quality jobs in Singapore. The managers have strong track records in regional markets and are committed to continue making significant allocations to Singapore as an integral part of their investment strategies," says Chee.

"They bring with them global distribution networks, sources of capital, and expertise that strengthen the depth and dynamism of our public markets," he adds.

See also: SGX RegCo rolls out enhanced disclosures to drive value creation

'You still have a chance'

MAS is also reviewing the proposals for a fourth batch of asset managers and announce this next year.

"For the local and international fund managers which have not been appointed, I would say, 'you still have a chance'. So please continue to engage MAS and share your proposals with us," says Chee.

At the same time, MAS has also committed $20 million from the Financial Sector Development Fund (FSDF) to the Grant for Equity Market Singapore (GEMS) Scheme to enhance equities market making activities in Singapore.

See also: EQDP fund manager Eastspring Investments launches new Singapore Income and Growth Equity Fund

According to Chee, this new GEMS Market Making Grant will strengthen Singapore's market making ecosystem, improve trading efficiency and execution quality, and increase the number of institutional grade stocks.

The aim is to raise trading interest in SGX-listed stocks and support greater demand through improved execution efficiency.

Chee says this grant will both the "middle segment" of small- and mid-cap stocks with sufficient trading activity, and also new listings.

"The aim is to improve trading liquidity and narrow the execution costs of these stocks," says Chee, who expects around 80 stocks outside the Straits Times Index (STI) to benefit from this scheme.

"Together, these efforts will deepen institutional and retail participation in Singapore equities, making our public markets a more effective destination for listings, financing, and exits within the broader capital ecosystem," he says.

Pang Qi Lim, CEO of HSBC Asset Management Singapore and Head of Strategic Partnerships for South East Asia, says he is excited to contribute to the continued development and internationalisation of Singapore’s equity market.

"Bringing together HSBC Asset Management’s investment capabilities and the bank’s deep institutional banking and wealth network, with both local and global reach – we are uniquely positioned to connect clients across markets to trade, invest, grow, and manage risk internationally," says Pang.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

"We look forward to leveraging these strengths to attract capital, broaden investor participation to further support the growth of a more vibrant and internationally connected equity market," he adds.

Manraj Sekhon, CEO of Templeton Asset Management and CIO of Templeton Global Investments says he is "delighted" with this opportunity to unlock the investment potential of Singapore equities and develop innovative products and structures.

"Franklin Templeton’s long history in Singapore, deep roots across Asia and global investment platform put us in a distinctive position to turn that ambition into action," he adds.

His colleague, Rene Buehlmann, head of APAC at Franklin Templeton, says this appointment reinforces the firm's longstanding commitment to the market and our conviction in its continued growth potential. "We are grateful for the confidence placed in us and look forward to supporting the continued development of Singapore’s capital markets."

title: Oil extends gain as Iran uncertainty outweighs Saudi pipe return
article:
(Sept 29): Oil rose for a second day as a lack of progress in US-Iran talks and signs of strong demand outweighed a resumption of flows through a key pipeline from top exporter Saudi Arabia.

Brent traded near US$107 a barrel after ticking higher in the previous session, while West Texas Intermediate headed toward US$94. Iranian officials have privately expressed pessimism about reaching a deal to end hostilities with Washington and reopen the Strait of Hormuz before US midterm elections in November, following US President Donald Trump’s rejection of a proposal to resume full traffic through the waterway in seven days.

Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia has restored about half the flows through its cross-country East-West pipeline, a crucial route bypassing the strait, after drone strikes halted operations earlier this month. Flows through the link to the Red Sea have reached at least 3.5 million barrels a day, according to people familiar with the matter.

“There’s still enormous geopolitical risk, but the market has learned that barrels keep finding a way out,” said Haris Khurshid, chief investment officer at Karobaar Capital LP. “We’re not seeing the kind of sustained repricing you’d expect if traders thought physical supply was about to deteriorate materially.”

Crude is headed for a third monthly gain on the escalating US-Iran tensions, disruptions to the Saudi bypass route and potential diesel export curbs by Washington. Brent is up more than 70% this year, after more than seven months of conflict in the Middle East.

Trump denied an Axios report that he offered Iran sanctions relief and the release of frozen funds in exchange for concrete steps on its nuclear programme. The Islamic Republic’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also refuted that Tehran was prepared to show flexibility on the nuclear issue, according to state news agency IRNA.

See also: Saudi Arabia’s key oil pipeline starts exports after repairs

Brent faces greater downside than upside risk, Khurshid said. A credible US-Iran deal would potentially shave as much as US$15 off prices, while US$120 a barrel would require an actual supply disruption, he added.

However, key gauges of supply tightness have spiked in recent days in a sign of a clamour for barrels that can be delivered quickly. Meanwhile, fuel prices are surging as global refinery capacity remains hobbled.

Brent’s prompt spread — the difference between its two nearest contracts — has widened to more than US$7 a barrel, from less than US$1 at the end of last month. The bullish pattern, known as backwardation, is a classic indicator of a tight market. In Europe, Dated Brent — a critical physical-market benchmark — has been trading at a wide premium to futures.

See also: Trump says he’s ‘very seriously’ looking at diesel export ban

Separately, TotalEnergies SE chief executive officer Patrick Pouyanné said a US ban on diesel exports being considered by Trump to curb high prices could backfire by pushing up gasoline costs. “It’s a bad idea” as it forces the nation’s refineries to cut throughput, potentially driving up domestic gasoline prices, he said.
• Brent for November settlement rose 1.4% to US$106.72 a barrel at 10.13am in Singapore.
• November futures expire on Wednesday. The more-active December contract advanced 1.5% to US$99.26 a barrel.

title: Goldman's John Waldron edges closer to succeeding Solomon as CEO
article:
(Sept 29): A year after Goldman Sachs Group Inc’s board offered John Waldron US$80 million to stay for the top job, it’s moving to ensure he doesn’t wait too long.

The board has discussed a plan where Waldron, who is currently chief operating officer, would succeed David Solomon as CEO as early as next year, the Wall Street Journal reported.

It’s becoming more apparent that Waldron, 57, long seen as the likely successor, is nearing the final step in his rise to the top of Goldman. Last year, the board telegraphed its view of Waldron’s future when it gave him a restricted stock package now worth nearly US$120 million to stay five more years — matching the incentive given to Solomon.

But the timing has remained unclear. Solomon, 64, has been in the job for eight years. And while his early-tenure push into the consumer business faltered, the bank’s been riding high in the years since, with its equity-trading desk hitting record after record and its investment bankers reeling in the highest fees since 2021.

With the latest plan, Waldron could take over toward the end of 2027 or in 2028, the Journal said, citing people familiar with the matter whom it didn’t identify. Solomon would likely become executive chairman for about one or two years after he steps down as CEO.

“Of course the board regularly discusses succession, as we disclose in our filings, but there is no definitive timeline for succession at Goldman Sachs,” Tony Fratto, a bank spokesman, said in an emailed statement. “Any assertions about timing are just speculation.”

See also: South Korea’s three-year yield rises to highest level since 2022

Waldron, who is also Goldman’s president, joined the bank back in 2000 and has steadily risen. He ran the media and entertainment banking group before becoming a head of leveraged finance.

He’s also worked closely with Solomon throughout his career. In 2014, Waldron was elevated to head the investment bank alongside Solomon and Richard Gnodde.

When Solomon was named CEO in 2018, he tapped Waldron for the coveted second-most important position at the bank.

See also: Rising fuel costs drive up brewing costs in Asia, Heineken says

“We are a close-knit group, who grew up together in the firm,” Waldron said at the bank’s investor day in 2020. “We now have a unique opportunity to lead this great institution forward.”

As president, Waldron has overseen key initiatives at Goldman to spur collaboration across the firm and drive gains from efficiency in artificial intelligence. He’s also pushed to grow the firm’s footprint outside of major financial hubs worldwide, helping cut costs and expand its talent pool.

In an CNBC interview in May, he described Goldman as a “human assembly line” that was ripe for automation from AI.

“Our human assembly lines will become more digitised, digital agents will be our robots,” Waldron said. “I’m not sure dynamically how the overall headcount will change, but I think the firm is going to get much more resilient and much more scalable.”

title: Mapletree Industrial Trust to divest 3255 Neil Armstrong Boulevard at US$9.8 mil, 10% below independent valuation
article:
Mapletree Industrial Trust (MIT) announced that it has entered into a sales and purchase agreement for the divestment of 3255 Neil Armstrong Boulevard, located in the US to DataBank Properties, LLC, which is the current tenant of the property, for a total consideration of US$9.81 million ($12.54 million).

The property is a single-storey building with a net lettable area of about 87,402 sq ft and is sited on freehold land with a land area of about 343,253 sq ft.

The manager states that the sale price was determined pursuant to the pricing mechanism set out in the lease agreement. While the sale price represents a 9% premium above MIT’s purchase price of US$9.0 million, it is 10% below the independent valuation of US$10.9 million as at March 31.

The property contributed about 0.2% to MIT’s portfolio gross revenue in the financial year ended March 31.

The manager expects the proposed divestment to be completed by the fourth quarter of 2026 and the net proceeds may be used to pare down debts and fund working capital requirements.

As at 9.41am, Units in MIT was trading 1 cent lower, or down 0.53% at $1.86.

title: Treasuries stabilise after sell-off, stocks slip
article:
(Sept 29): Bond investors got a respite in early Asian trading from a bruising sell-off after surging oil prices and mounting bets on further Federal Reserve (Fed) interest-rate hikes drove Treasury yields to multi-year highs. Asian stocks fell.

The US 10-year yield was little changed at 5.23% after climbing as much as 11 basis points on Monday to the highest since 2007. Two- and 30-year yields were also little changed as traders braced for the Fed to keep tightening policy to rein in inflation. Australian government bonds held steady before a central bank monetary policy decision later Tuesday.

Brent crude advanced for a second day, climbing 1.1% to US$106.44 a barrel, as optimism for an imminent diplomatic breakthrough in the Middle East faded. Gold was little changed around US$4,118 an ounce after slumping almost 4% on Monday.

MSCI’s Asia Pacific share index declined 0.3%, with losses in South Korea and Japan. Equity-index futures for Wall Street benchmarks slipped 0.1%.

Climbing oil prices have weighed on global bond markets by keeping inflation risks alive and reinforcing expectations that interest rates will stay higher for longer. In the US, stronger business activity and concerns over elevated government debt levels have fuelled the biggest Treasury sell-off since US President Donald Trump’s April 2025 tariff rollout rattled markets.

“The broader market hasn’t been able to gain much traction because of rising yields and oil prices,” said Chris Larkin at E*Trade from Morgan Stanley. “With the Fed focused on the inflation side of its mandate, unless this week’s labour-market data is a major surprise, it will likely play second fiddle to interest rates and energy.”

See also: Bonds drop with stocks as Iran tensions boost oil

Iran and the US remained far apart on a ceasefire and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran sticking to a proposal Trump has rejected. Trump denied an Axios report that he’s willing to offer sanctions relief and release frozen Iranian funds in exchange “for concrete nuclear concessions”.

Iranian officials have privately expressed pessimism about reaching an agreement to end hostilities and reopen the strait before the US midterm elections in November, according to people familiar with the matter.

“Our expectations remain that the conflict will be with markets for the foreseeable future and the global economy will continue adjusting to the realities of the supply disruptions,” said Ian Lyngen at BMO Capital Markets.

Investors will also be watching a packed slate of US economic data this week for signs the economy remains strong enough to support further Fed tightening. Consumer confidence and August JOLTS figures are due Tuesday, followed by consumer-spending and inflation data and then payrolls on Friday.

“If economic resilience and investment demand remain intact, there may still be scope for yields to move higher,” said Seema Shah at Principal Asset Management.
